items.text: At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward.

paragraphs.before: Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding an Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding.
paragraphs.window: At first, it’s deliberate, even awkward.
paragraphs.after: With time, the roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

section: The Chicken-and-Egg Problem
Five Stages of Reparenting

paragraphs.before: 1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting:2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
paragraphs.after: Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them. 5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!

section: My Journey
Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
Signs of Manipulation

paragraphs.before: Some manipulative people are too smart to act perfect. They lead with their wounds, or with how brutally honest they are about their flaws (very disarming, which is sort of the point), and every warning you hear about them just becomes more proof of how deep they are.
paragraphs.window: Your Protector has to catch the moment compassion starts explaining away what you’ve already seen.
paragraphs.after: “I have honesty issues and I’m working on them” may be a perfectly honest thing to say. It’s also telling you there’s an honesty problem right now, and knowing about a problem isn’t fixing it.

section: Before You Try to Go Deep
When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

paragraphs.before: This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who’s horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they’d rather not have sometimes, and they don’t make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you’re calm and actually ready.
paragraphs.window: A real parent doesn’t get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be a perfect one.

items.text: Ask what a minimally competent adult would do here.
section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow One Competency at a Time
For protecting

paragraphs.window: Ask what a minimally competent adult would do here.
paragraphs.after: Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!

section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Remember When You Already Did It

paragraphs.before: My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with.

section: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care

paragraphs.window: Watch how it lands, though.
paragraphs.after: “I care about you” can be patient, or it can be “I care about you, now hurry up and feel better.” Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who’s just sitting there. And if nothing moves at all, don’t push it. Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you’re borrowing something you already know how to do.

When Healing Turns Into Checking

paragraphs.window: Going back can still matter, even when nothing new turns up.
paragraphs.after: But returning to the same wound can also become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence. Spending all day asking, “Did I process it properly? Did I grieve it enough?” is clearly not what we’re after here.

items.text: And the checking doesn’t always stay in your head.
section: Building Trust With Your Little One
When Healing Turns Into Checking

paragraphs.window: And the checking doesn’t always stay in your head.
paragraphs.after: A body scan can turn into one, or a confession. Even, going on a date, or checking your dating profile matches, can be a version of this if what you’re really after is proof that you’re good and lovable. It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.

section: Simple Practices
A Heart-to-Child Loop

paragraphs.before: Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part’s a gift from them, and they don’t owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours.
paragraphs.window: No warmth today?
paragraphs.after: Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time.

section: Appendix

paragraphs.window: Where it really differs is spirituality.
paragraphs.after: Schema therapy doesn’t build it in, though the preface to its main textbook calls blending it with meditation or religious practice an important development. That’s not so surprising, since it grew out of cognitive therapy. Some people do blend them, though. Tara Bennett-Goleman’s book Emotional Alchemy, for one, fits a Buddhist loving-kindness wish to each schema. Her book barely mentions gratitude, and for me that’s the door to the bigger love back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! IFS goes overboard the other way, in my opinion (more on that in the next section).
